title: Balfour v. Balfour
summary: A husband’s promise of a temporary living allowance while the spouses remained amicably married did not establish the contractual obligation the wife sought to enforce.
notes: [1919] 2 K.B. 571 (C.A.), decided 25 June 1919. Atkin L.J. reasoned that agreements between spouses living in amity are presumed not to be intended to create legal relations, and that enforcing them would flood the courts; Warrington L.J. rested on the absence of any bargain by the wife, and Duke L.J. warned that enforcing such domestic promises would be a fruitful source of dissension.

sections.Parties: Mrs. Balfour sued her husband for unpaid maintenance allegedly promised by contract. Mr. Balfour was a civil servant working in Ceylon, where they had lived together before their visit to England.
sections.Material Facts: The spouses married in 1900 and came to England in 1915 while the husband was on leave. When he returned to Ceylon in August 1916, the wife stayed behind on medical advice because she had rheumatic arthritis. They calculated her living expenses together. He gave her money for part of August and promised £30 per month until she rejoined him. She initially intended to return, and the arrangement was made before the subsequent marital disagreements. Later he suggested that they remain apart. She obtained a decree for restitution of conjugal rights and an alimony order in separate proceedings. Her contract suit depended on treating the earlier allowance arrangement as an enforceable bargain.
sections.Procedural History: Sargant J. entered judgment for the wife, treating her acceptance of the fixed allowance as consideration for a binding agreement. In 1919 the Court of Appeal allowed the husband’s appeal and entered judgment for him. Warrington, Duke, and Atkin each gave reasons. The contract disposition must be distinguished from the separate marital maintenance proceedings.
sections.Issue: Did the spouses’ allowance arrangement manifest a legally enforceable bargain, supported by consideration, rather than a domestic arrangement responsive to changing family circumstances?
sections.Holding: No contract on the terms alleged was established. The appeal succeeded. The judges agreed on the result while emphasizing somewhat different deficiencies in the alleged bargain and its intended legal effect.
sections.Reasoning:
Warrington asked what the wife had actually promised in return. It was implausible that she had committed to accept £30 under every future circumstance, whatever her illness or needs, while the husband committed to that sum regardless of his own circumstances. Their discussion concerned what was presently necessary for maintenance; it did not establish those reciprocal contractual commitments. Duke likewise found no contractual consideration in a supposed surrender of authority to pledge the husband’s credit, an authority dependent on the marital relationship and its circumstances. He distinguished agreements genuinely made upon separation from this arrangement made while the spouses remained in amity.

Atkin explained that agreements may contain promises and even apparent consideration without being intended to create legal consequences. Ordinary domestic arrangements commonly depend on affection, mutual accommodation, and changing needs. Their context therefore matters to the objective legal meaning of the exchange. On these facts, the spouses did not intend the rigid obligation the suit asserted. The wife bore the burden of proving a contract and had not discharged it.

learning.why: Balfour separates a seriously intended promise to provide support from an intention to create the particular legal obligation claimed. Read it with Lucy and Cohen, while keeping its historical marital setting visible.

topics.assent: The setting of an agreement affects whether words and conduct communicate contractual commitment.
topics.intent-to-be-bound: An intended promise of support does not necessarily carry an intention to create the rigid legal obligation asserted.
topics.consideration: The judges question what legally sufficient return promise the wife supplied.
topics.social-intent: Balfour is the leading authority that ordinary domestic arrangements between spouses are presumed not intended to have legal consequences.
topics.assent-consent-intent: The case separates factual agreement from intent to be legally bound, which the court found lacking.

learning.separateOpinions: All three judges concurred in allowing the appeal. Warrington focused on the absence of the reciprocal bargain alleged; Duke emphasized consideration and the continuing marital relationship; Atkin explained the absence of intended legal consequences in ordinary domestic arrangements.

mnemonic.rationale: A husband’s allowance the law would not enforce
